questions.question:
The statement [latex]( eg p)\Rightarrow ( eg q)[/latex] is logically equivalent to which of the statements below?
I. [latex] p\Rightarrow q [/latex]
II. [latex]q \Rightarrow p [/latex]
III. [latex]( eg q)\vee p[/latex]
IV. [latex]( eg p)\vee q[/latex]

[latex] eg p\Rightarrow eg q[/latex] is the contrapositive of [latex]q\Rightarrow p[/latex], so they are equivalent (II). Also [latex]a\Rightarrow b\equiv eg a\vee b[/latex], so [latex] eg p\Rightarrow eg q\equiv p\vee eg q[/latex] (III).

I ([latex]p\Rightarrow q[/latex]) and IV ([latex] eg p\vee q[/latex]) are the converse, which is different.

Answer: II and III only

questions.question:
Let G be an arbitrary group. Consider the following relations on G:

R1: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_1b[/latex] if and only if [latex]\exists g \in G[/latex] such that [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex]
R2: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_2b[/latex] if and only if [latex]a=b^{-1}[/latex]

Which of the above is/are equivalence relation/relations?
questions.explanation:
R1 (conjugacy):
- Reflexive: [latex]a=e^{-1}ae[/latex]
- Symmetric: if [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex] then [latex]b=gag^{-1}[/latex]
- Transitive: [latex]a=g^{-1}bg,\ b=h^{-1}ch\Rightarrow a=(hg)^{-1}c(hg)[/latex]
So R1 is an equivalence relation.

R2: aR2a would need [latex]a=a^{-1}[/latex], which fails in general (e.g. 1 in [latex]\mathbb{Z}_3[/latex]). Not reflexive.

Answer: R1 only

questions.question:
Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected graph. A vertex cover of [latex]G[/latex] is a subset [latex]V^{\prime} \subseteq V[/latex] such that for every [latex](u, v) \in E, u \in V^{\prime}[/latex] or [latex]v \in V^{\prime}[/latex]. Let the size of the smallest vertex cover in [latex]G[/latex] be [latex]k[/latex]. Let [latex]S[/latex] be any vertex cover of size [latex]k[/latex].

For a vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], which of the following constraints will always ensure that [latex]v \in S[/latex] ?

options.A: The degree of [latex]v[/latex] is at least [latex]k+1[/latex]
options.B: The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is on a path of length [latex]k+1[/latex]
options.C: The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is on a cycle of length [latex]k+1[/latex]
options.D: The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is a part of a clique of size [latex]k[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Suppose, for contradiction, [latex]v[/latex] has degree [latex]\ge k+1[/latex] but [latex]v\notin S[/latex] for some minimum vertex cover [latex]S[/latex] of size [latex]k[/latex]. Since [latex]v\notin S[/latex], every edge incident on [latex]v[/latex] must be covered by its other endpoint (because [latex]S[/latex] is a vertex cover), so all [latex]\ge k+1[/latex] distinct neighbors of [latex]v[/latex] must belong to [latex]S[/latex]. But then [latex]|S|\ge k+1>k[/latex], contradicting that [latex]S[/latex] has size exactly [latex]k[/latex]. So [latex]v[/latex] must be in every minimum vertex cover.

The other conditions don't force inclusion: a vertex on a long path or cycle can often be excluded by choosing the cover among its neighbors instead; and being part of a size-[latex]k[/latex] clique only forces [latex]k-1[/latex] of the clique's vertices into the cover (any one clique vertex, including [latex]v[/latex], can be the one left out).

Answer: "The degree of v is at least k+1" always forces v ∈ S.

questions.question:
Consider the following relation on subsets of the set S of integers between 1 and 2014. For two distinct subsets U and V of S we say U[latex]\lt[/latex]V if the minimum element in the symmetric difference of the two sets is in U.
Consider the following two statements:
S1: There is a subset of S that is larger than every other subset.
S2: There is a subset of S that is smaller than every other subset.
Which one of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are true
options.B: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.C: S2 is true and S1 is false
options.D: Neither S1 nor S2 is true

questions.explanation:
U [latex]\lt[/latex] V when the smallest element of [latex]U\triangle V[/latex] lies in U.

- Take U = S (the full set). For any V [latex]\ne[/latex] S, [latex]S\triangle V=S-V[/latex], whose minimum is in S. So S is smaller than every other subset [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S2 true.
- Take V = [latex]\emptyset[/latex]. For any U, [latex]U\triangle\emptyset=U[/latex], minimum in U, so U [latex]\lt\emptyset[/latex]. So [latex]\emptyset[/latex] is larger than every other subset [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S1 true.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true

questions.question:
[latex] A = \{ 0,1,2,3,\dots \} [/latex] is the set of non-negative integers. Let [latex] {F} [/latex] be the set of functions from [latex] A [/latex] to itself. For any two functions, [latex] f_1, f_2 \in {F} [/latex], we define

[latex] (f_1 \odot f_2)(n) = f_1(n) + f_2(n)[/latex]

for every number [latex] n [/latex] in [latex] A [/latex]. Which of the following is/are CORRECT about the mathematical structure [latex] ({F}, \odot ) [/latex]?
questions.explanation:
[latex](f_1\odot f_2)(n)=f_1(n)+f_2(n)[/latex] — pointwise addition of functions into the non-negative integers.

- Closure: the sum of two non-negative-integer values is still a non-negative integer, so [latex]F[/latex] is closed under [latex]\odot[/latex].
- Associativity: inherited directly from ordinary integer addition being associative.
- Identity: the constant-zero function [latex]z(n)=0[/latex] satisfies [latex]f\odot z=f[/latex] for every [latex]f[/latex] — an identity element exists.
- Commutativity: [latex]f_1(n)+f_2(n)=f_2(n)+f_1(n)[/latex] pointwise, so [latex]\odot[/latex] is commutative.
- Inverses: for a general [latex]f[/latex] (e.g. [latex]f(n)=n[/latex]), we'd need some [latex]g[/latex] with [latex]f(n)+g(n)=0[/latex], forcing [latex]g(n)=-f(n)[/latex] — but negative values aren't allowed in the codomain [latex]A[/latex]. So inverses generally don't exist.

Since it's closed, associative, has an identity, and is commutative, but lacks inverses, [latex](F,\odot)[/latex] is exactly an Abelian monoid (not a group).

Answer: (F, ⊙) is an Abelian monoid.

questions.question:
Let [latex] f:A\rightarrow B[/latex] be an onto (or surjective) function, where [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are nonempty sets. Define an equivalence relation [latex] \sim [/latex] on the set [latex]A[/latex] as
[latex] a_1\sim a_2 \text{ if } f(a_1)=f(a_2),[/latex]
where [latex] a_1, a_2 \in A[/latex] . Let [latex] \varepsilon =\{[x]:x \in A\}[/latex] be the set of all the equivalence classes under [latex] \sim [/latex]. Define a new mapping [latex] F: \varepsilon \rightarrow B[/latex] as
[latex]F([x]) = f(x),[/latex] for all the equivalence classes [latex][x][/latex] in [latex] \varepsilon[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.B: F is an onto (or surjective) function.
options.C: F is a one-to-one (or injective) function.

questions.explanation:
Check each property of F:
- Well-defined: if [x] = [y], then f(x) = f(y), so F gives the same value for every representative (option 1 FALSE).
- Onto: for any b in B, f is onto, so f(a) = b for some a, and F([a]) = b.
- One-to-one: F([x]) = F([y]) means f(x) = f(y), so [latex]x\sim y[/latex] and [x] = [y].
- Onto and one-to-one [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] bijective.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.question:
A relation [latex]R[/latex] is said to be circular if [latex]aRb[/latex] and [latex]bRc[/latex] together imply [latex]cRa[/latex].
Which of the following options is/are correct?

options.A: If a relation S is reflexive and symmetric, then S is an equivalence relation.
options.B: If a relation S is circular and symmetric, then S is an equivalence relation.
options.C: If a relation S is reflexive and circular, then S is an equivalence relation.
options.D: If a relation S is transitive and circular, then S is an equivalence relation.

questions.explanation:
Reflexive + circular gives an equivalence relation:
- Symmetric: aRb and bRb (reflexive) [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] bRa (circular).
- Transitive: aRb and bRc [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] cRa (circular) [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] aRc (symmetric).

The others fail: reflexive + symmetric need not be transitive; circular + symmetric need not be reflexive (e.g. the empty relation); transitive + circular need not be reflexive either.

Answer: Reflexive and circular [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] equivalence relation
